cards.title: SLI — What You Actually Measure
cards.teaser: A Service Level Indicator is a carefully chosen quantitative measure of some aspect of the service's behavior. The choice of SLI is not a measurement question — it is a product question: what property, if degraded, makes users unhappy?

runs.text: Google's SRE Book defines a
Service Level Indicator (SLI)
as "a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service that is provided." The definition looks simple, but the word "carefully" is doing a lot of work.

Most teams measure what is easy to instrument: CPU utilization, memory usage, container restart counts, queue depths. These are server-side metrics. An SLI is different — it measures the service from the user's perspective. The SRE Book frames it precisely: the right SLIs are the ones that measure
user happiness
, not server health.
The most common SLI categories described in the SRE Workbook:

items.text: — the proportion of requests served successfully. Expressed as a ratio: good requests / total requests. "A request is good if it returns HTTP 2xx or 3xx within 500ms."
— the proportion of requests served faster than a threshold. "90% of checkout page loads complete in under 300ms."
— the proportion of requests served with full feature fidelity (not degraded). Used when graceful degradation is possible — serving cached or partial results when a dependency is slow.
— for data pipelines and caches: the proportion of reads returning data less than X minutes old.
— the proportion of operations producing the correct result. Used for data processing systems where wrong output is worse than slow output.

runs.text: An SLI is always a
ratio

of good events to total events, expressed as a proportion between 0 and 1 (or 0% to 100%). Raw counts — "we had 47 errors today" — are not SLIs; they cannot be compared across periods of different traffic volume.

Source: Betsy Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (Google, 2016), Chapter 4: Service Level Objectives. The SRE Workbook (2018) refines the SLI/SLO/error budget model with worked examples across request/response services, data pipelines, and storage systems.

An SLI is a single number that answers: "out of all the things users asked us to do in this time window, what fraction went well?" It is always a ratio — good events divided by total events — measured from the user's point of view, not the server's.

cards.title: Picking Good SLIs — Measure User Happiness
cards.teaser: The hardest part of SLI design is not instrumentation — it is deciding what "good" means to a user. The wrong SLI gives you a green dashboard while users are suffering. The right SLI makes user pain impossible to hide.

runs.text: The SRE Workbook describes a concrete process for choosing SLIs: start with the user journey, identify the critical interactions, and ask what property of each interaction, if degraded, would make the user notice or complain. That property is your SLI candidate.
Common traps in SLI selection:

items.text: CPU utilization at 90% does not tell you if users are experiencing slowness. Latency at the 99th percentile does. Instrument the outcome.
If a service has 20 SLIs, on-call engineers cannot reason about service health quickly. The SRE Workbook recommends 1-3 SLIs per service, covering the most user-visible properties.
A request that returns HTTP 200 after 30 seconds is technically "available" but useless. A good availability SLI definition includes a latency threshold: "returns 2xx within 1000ms."
Error cases that users hit frequently should be included in the SLI. A search that returns HTTP 500 on malformed queries affects real users, even if the request is technically "invalid."

runs.text: A practical test for any SLI candidate: imagine the SLI is at 100% — does that mean all users are perfectly happy? If yes, it is a candidate. If you can imagine users complaining despite a 100% SLI, you are measuring the wrong thing.

Where to measure: the SRE Workbook recommends measuring SLIs as close to the user as possible — at the load balancer or API gateway, not deep inside a microservice. Internal service latency that never reaches users should not count against your SLI.

The four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) from the SRE Book are a useful starting point, but they are diagnostic signals — not SLIs. An SLI is a curated ratio derived from those signals, calibrated to user experience, not a raw metric.

Pick the SLI that, if it dropped to 50%, you would immediately hear from users. If you can't imagine users noticing, you're measuring the wrong thing. Start with the user's experience, work backward to the metric.

cards.title: SLO — The Target Value
cards.teaser: A Service Level Objective is a target value or range for an SLI. It is the number your team commits to maintaining. Setting it too high wastes engineering resources on over-engineering. Setting it too low fails users. The right SLO is the one that matches user expectations.

runs.text: An
SLO (Service Level Objective)

is a statement of the form: "the SLI will be at or above X% over measurement period Y." For example: "99.9% of API requests complete successfully in under 500ms, measured over a rolling 28-day window."
The SLO has several components, each of which must be specified:

items.text: Availability? Latency? Correctness? Be precise about what counts as a "good" event.
99%? 99.9%? 99.99%? Each additional nine costs exponentially more to achieve and maintain.
Rolling 28 days? Calendar month? Quarter? The window determines how quickly SLO breaches are detected and how quickly the budget resets.
Does planned maintenance count against the SLO? Do health check requests count? Does synthetic traffic count? Specify explicitly to avoid disputes during incidents.

runs.text: The SRE Book's guidance on setting the right SLO target: start by asking users directly what level of service they notice and care about. Then set the SLO slightly below your current performance level. This creates an error budget you can actually spend, rather than an aspirational target that leaves your team perpetually in breach.

SLOs should be owned by the engineering team, not by a contract or by management. The SRE Workbook is explicit: SLOs are an engineering tool for making tradeoffs. When the SLO is imposed from outside rather than chosen by the team, engineers lose the incentive to use it as a real engineering signal.

A useful distinction from the SRE Workbook: an SLO is what you target internally; an SLA (Service Level Agreement) is what you promise contractually. SLOs are typically set tighter than SLAs — if your SLA is 99.9%, your internal SLO might be 99.95%, giving you a buffer before you breach the contractual commitment.

An SLO is the answer to: "what percentage of the time must this service be good enough?" It is a target number with a time window attached. If you are below it, something must change. If you are well above it, you may be over-engineering reliability.

cards.title: SLA — The Contractual SLO
cards.teaser: An SLA is an SLO with legal and financial consequences attached. The gap between your internal SLO and your external SLA is intentional — it is the buffer that prevents a near-miss from becoming a breach of contract.

runs.text: A
Service Level Agreement (SLA)

is a formal, often contractual commitment to customers specifying the minimum level of service and the consequences of falling below it. Consequences are typically financial: service credits, refunds, or contract termination clauses.
The SLI / SLO / SLA hierarchy:

items.text: — what you measure (e.g., request success rate).
— what you target internally (e.g., 99.95% over 28 days). Owned by engineering.
— what you promise contractually (e.g., 99.9% over a calendar month). Owned by sales, legal, and product.

runs.text: Setting SLAs tighter than SLOs is a structural error. If the SLA is 99.9% and the internal SLO is also 99.9%, any SLO miss immediately triggers SLA consequences — there is no margin to detect the problem and respond before it becomes a legal issue.

The SRE Book recommends that SLAs never be set so tight that they are automatically triggered by a single production incident. Common practice: set the SLA at least one nine below the internal SLO target (e.g., SLO 99.9%, SLA 99.5%). The gap absorbs normal operational variance.

SLAs also differ from SLOs in measurement period: SLAs are often defined over calendar months (matching billing cycles), while SLOs use rolling windows. These two windows can diverge — an outage at the end of one calendar month and the start of the next may look acceptable within the SLA while clearly breaching the rolling-window SLO.

Not every service needs an SLA. Internal services within an organization typically need SLOs but rarely need formal SLAs. Reserve SLAs for externally-facing services where customers have commercial expectations and there are financial consequences for breach.
SLA is the promise you make to customers in a contract. SLO is the tighter internal target you hold yourself to so you never breach that promise. The gap between them is your safety margin.

cards.title: SLO Math — The Nines Table
cards.teaser: The "nines" notation (99%, 99.9%, 99.99%) translates directly into allowed downtime per year. Each additional nine reduces your error budget by ~10x. Understanding the math prevents both over-engineering and under-promising.

runs.text: SLO targets are typically expressed in "nines" — the number of 9s in the percentage. A 99.9% SLO is called "three nines." The math translates availability percentages into concrete downtime budgets that make the engineering tradeoffs tangible.
The nines table (per year and per 30-day month):
The formula:
allowed downtime = (1 - SLO_fraction) × seconds_in_window
The cost implications are critical. Going from 99.9% to 99.99% is not 10% harder — it requires eliminating roughly 90% of your current downtime. Each additional nine typically requires:

items.text: — at five nines, a human cannot even respond in time.

runs.text: Five nines (99.999%) allows only 5.26 minutes of downtime per year. A single deployment that takes 3 minutes consumes 57% of the annual error budget. At this level, every deploy must be zero-downtime, and every incident response must be automated. Very few services outside telephony and financial clearing truly need five nines.

99.9% sounds great, but it means you are allowed to be down for 40 minutes every month. 99.99% cuts that to 4 minutes. Each extra nine multiplies the cost roughly 10x. Before chasing another nine, ask: does the cost of achieving it match the user harm you are preventing?

cards.title: Error Budget — The Engineering Room to Take Risks
cards.teaser: An error budget is the complement of an SLO: the amount of unreliability you are allowed to have. It transforms reliability from a constraint into a resource — one you can spend on risky deployments, experiments, and infrastructure changes.

runs.text: The
error budget
is defined as:
error budget = 1 - SLO
. If your SLO is 99.9%, your error budget is 0.1% — that is, 0.1% of requests are allowed to fail, or equivalently, the service is allowed to be degraded for 43.8 minutes per 30-day window.

The insight that makes error budgets powerful is reframing: instead of asking "how do we avoid all incidents?", the team asks "how do we wisely spend our error budget?" This reframe has concrete implications:

items.text: — as long as the team expects the risk to consume less error budget than the feature is worth.
Load testing in production is acceptable
— if the team chooses to spend some error budget learning about system behavior.
Infrastructure migrations are negotiated, not blocked
— the team can do disruptive work as long as total error budget consumption stays within the SLO.

runs.text: The error budget is consumed by:

items.text: Risky deployments that partially degrade service.
Planned maintenance (if included in SLI measurement).
Performance degradation that crosses the SLI threshold.

runs.text: The SRE Book frames the error budget as the cornerstone of the SRE / product team relationship: when the error budget is healthy, product velocity is prioritized; when the error budget is exhausted, reliability work is prioritized. This mechanism removes the perpetual negotiation between speed and stability — the budget adjudicates it objectively.

Error budgets work best when both the product team and the SRE team use the same budget number. If engineering tracks SLOs internally but product teams are not shown the error budget consumption, the mechanism loses its value as a negotiating tool.

An error budget is the unreliability you are allowed to have before you breach your SLO. If your SLO is 99.9%, your error budget is 0.1% — think of it as 40 minutes of downtime to spend each month however you want: risky deploys, experiments, or just bad luck. When it runs out, you stop spending and focus on reliability.

cards.title: Error Budget Policy — What Happens When You Exhaust It
cards.teaser: An error budget without a policy is a number on a dashboard. An error budget policy is the pre-agreed response to exhaustion: what the team does differently when the budget runs out, and who has authority to override it.

runs.text: The
error budget policy

is a document — agreed in advance between the SRE team, the development team, and product leadership — that specifies the team's response at various budget consumption levels. The SRE Workbook describes this as one of the most important artifacts for making SRE work in practice.
A typical policy has three trigger levels:

items.text: Normal operations. Feature velocity is the priority. Risky changes may proceed with normal review.
Caution mode. Risky deployments require additional review. On-call engineering is notified of elevated burn rate. Reliability work is added to the backlog.

Feature freeze. No new feature deployments until the error budget resets or is replenished through a reliability investment. Incident retrospectives for all recent SLO-impacting events are completed. Leadership is notified.
Hard stop on feature work. Engineering sprint redirected to reliability. If the exhaustion was caused by a specific known issue, that issue is the P0 priority.

runs.text: The policy must also address:

items.text: Who can authorize a risky deployment when the budget is low? Under what circumstances? The policy should name a role (e.g., "Engineering Director approval required"), not a person.
Does the budget reset at the start of the measurement window automatically? Can it be credited back by completing a postmortem or implementing a specific reliability fix?
If the budget is exhausted in three consecutive windows, the SLO target itself should be reconsidered — either the service is too complex to meet the target, or the target was set too high.

runs.text: A policy that exists but is consistently overridden is worse than no policy. It signals that reliability commitments are not real, which destroys the trust of the SRE team and makes future SLO negotiations meaningless. Enforce the policy or explicitly revise it — do not quietly ignore it.

An error budget policy is the agreement you make before the crisis about what you will do when the crisis happens. It turns "we're out of error budget" from a judgment call in the moment into an automatic response that everyone already agreed to. Write it when things are calm; follow it when things are hot.

cards.title: The 28-Day Window — Rolling vs Calendar
cards.teaser: The measurement window for an SLO determines how quickly budget exhaustion is detected and how quickly it resets. A rolling 28-day window gives continuous visibility and avoids month-boundary artifacts that calendar windows produce.

runs.text: The SRE Workbook identifies the
measurement window
as one of the most consequential SLO design decisions. The two most common choices are a rolling 28-day window (Google's recommendation) and a calendar month window.

Why 28 days specifically? Because it is exactly four weeks, which makes week-over-week comparisons clean and avoids the varying lengths of calendar months (28 to 31 days). A consistent window allows meaningful trend analysis.
Rolling window vs calendar window:

items.text: — the window moves forward continuously. Today's SLO compliance is computed over the last 28 days at any moment. An incident from 3 weeks ago still affects current compliance until it ages out. This gives a realistic view of what users experienced recently.

— resets to 100% on the first of each month. An outage on January 31st has zero impact on February's SLO compliance. This creates perverse incentives: teams may be more willing to take risks late in a month ("it'll reset in two days anyway").

runs.text: The rolling window also avoids the "cliff effect" — a major incident at the start of a calendar month can make the entire month look bad, while the same incident at the end of the month barely registers before the reset. Rolling windows smooth this out.

Practical consideration: calendar windows are often used for SLAs because they align with billing cycles. When your SLO uses a rolling window and your SLA uses a calendar window, you must track both and ensure the rolling-window SLO provides sufficient buffer against calendar-month SLA breaches.

In Prometheus, a rolling 28-day window SLO compliance can be computed using a recording rule: rate(http_requests_total{code!~"5.."}[28d]) / rate(http_requests_total[28d]). This gives a continuously updated compliance ratio that reflects exactly the last 28 days of traffic.

A rolling 28-day window means your SLO compliance is always calculated against the last 28 days — it never resets artificially. A calendar-month window resets on the 1st of every month, which creates weird incentives near month-end. Rolling windows are more honest; calendar windows are easier to explain to customers.

cards.title: Burn Rate — Speed of Budget Consumption
cards.teaser: Burn rate measures how fast you are consuming your error budget relative to the rate that would exhaust it exactly at window end. A burn rate of 1 means you're on track to use the budget perfectly; above 1 means you'll exhaust it before the window closes.

runs.text: The
burn rate

concept comes from the SRE Workbook's alerting chapter and addresses a fundamental problem with SLO-based alerting: a service could be slowly accumulating errors that will exhaust the error budget by day 27 of a 28-day window — but no single alert threshold gets triggered because the instantaneous error rate looks acceptable.
Burn rate is defined as:
burn_rate = error_rate / (1 - SLO)

. For a 99.9% SLO (0.1% error budget), an error rate of 0.1% gives burn rate 1.0 (consuming budget at exactly the sustainable rate). An error rate of 1% gives burn rate 10 — the budget will be exhausted 10x faster than the window allows.
Worked example for a 99.9% SLO over 28 days:

items.text: — error rate 0.1%; budget exhausted at day 28. Normal operations.
— error rate 0.2%; budget exhausted at day 14.
— error rate 1.44%; budget exhausted in 2 hours. Requires an immediate page to on-call.
— error rate 3.6%; budget exhausted in 47 minutes. Major incident — requires immediate response.

Burn rate alerting was introduced in the SRE Workbook (Chapter 5: Alerting on SLOs) as a replacement for raw error-rate alerting. Raw error rate alerts fire on short spikes that do not materially harm the SLO; burn rate alerts fire when the consumption rate is genuinely threatening to exhaust the budget.

Burn rate is your error budget's speedometer. A burn rate of 1 means you are spending budget at exactly the sustainable pace. A burn rate of 14 means you'll be out of budget in a fraction of the time. When the burn rate is high enough that exhaustion is minutes away, you need someone paged immediately.

cards.title: Multi-Window Multi-Burn-Rate Alerting
cards.teaser: Google's SRE Workbook alerting recipe uses two burn rate thresholds and two time windows simultaneously — catching both fast-burning incidents and slow-burning degradations while minimizing alert noise and avoiding page exhaustion.

runs.text: Single-window burn-rate alerting has a fundamental problem: a short window (1 hour) is sensitive to brief spikes that recover quickly; a long window (24 hours) is slow to detect fast-moving incidents. The SRE Workbook's solution is
multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting
— alerting only when a high burn rate is sustained across both a short and a long window simultaneously.
The Workbook's recommended recipe for a 99.9% SLO over 30 days (2592000 seconds):

items.text: burn rate > 14.4 sustained over both 1h and 5m windows. This fires when an incident is consuming the monthly budget in under 2 hours. 2% of budget consumed in 5 minutes confirms the burn is real, not a spike.
burn rate > 6 sustained over both 6h and 30m windows. This fires when budget exhaustion is projected within about 5 days. Needs investigation within the hour.
burn rate > 3 sustained over both 24h and 2h windows. Budget exhaustion projected in about 10 days. Addressed in the next business day.
burn rate > 1 sustained over 3d window. Budget is being consumed faster than it replenishes. Investigate this week.

The two-window requirement is critical: it ensures the alert is not triggered by a brief spike (the 5m window may spike, but the 1h window will not confirm it unless the error rate has been sustained). This dramatically reduces alert noise compared to single-window approaches.

The full recipe is specified in the SRE Workbook, Chapter 5 ("Alerting on SLOs"). The Google SRE team validated that the four-level recipe (two pages + two tickets) catches >99% of budget-exhausting incidents with far lower false-positive rates than threshold-based or raw error-rate alerting.

Multi-window alerting says: only page me if the burn rate is high in both a long window AND a short window. The long window filters out noise; the short window confirms the incident is still happening right now. Two windows, two burn-rate thresholds — four alert levels covering everything from "fix this week" to "wake someone up immediately."

cards.title: Composite SLOs — Combining Multiple SLIs
cards.teaser: Many user journeys depend on multiple properties simultaneously: a page that loads fast but shows wrong data fails users just as much as one that shows correct data slowly. Composite SLOs combine multiple SLIs with AND logic, so any single failure counts against the budget.

runs.text: A
composite SLO

is an SLO that requires multiple SLI conditions to be simultaneously satisfied. The SRE Workbook describes two approaches: treating a request as "good" only if it satisfies all SLI criteria at once, or defining separate SLOs for each SLI and tracking them independently.

The most common composite SLO pattern combines availability and latency. For example: "A request is good if it returns HTTP 2xx AND completes in under 500ms." A request that returns HTTP 200 in 5 seconds is a bad event. A request that returns HTTP 500 in 50ms is a bad event. Only requests satisfying both conditions count as good.
Why this matters:

items.text: Separate SLOs can mask correlated failures.

If availability is at 99.95% and latency is at 99.93%, both look fine individually. But if the slow requests and the failed requests are the same requests, the fraction of requests that are good on both dimensions is lower than either SLO suggests.
A user who gets a slow successful response does not care that the availability SLO is green — they had a bad experience.

runs.text: The PromQL expression for a composite availability + latency SLI at a 99.9% SLO:

items.text: — good events are those with 2xx status AND within the 500ms histogram bucket.

runs.text: Beyond availability and latency, composite SLOs are used for data pipeline services that must satisfy both freshness (data is recent) and correctness (data is accurate). A pipeline result that is fresh but wrong, or correct but stale, counts as a bad event under the composite SLO.

Composite SLOs with more than 2-3 conditions become difficult to debug. When the SLO is breaching, "the composite SLO is unhealthy" does not tell on-call engineers which component is the problem. Ensure each SLI dimension is also tracked independently so engineers can quickly identify which component is causing the composite breach.

A composite SLO says a request is only "good" if it passes every SLI test at once — right AND fast, for example. It is harder to satisfy than any individual SLO, which is the point: users experience all dimensions simultaneously, so your SLO should reflect that.

cards.title: The 100% Trap — Why Perfect Reliability Is Anti-Economical
cards.teaser: Targeting 100% availability is not a reliability goal — it is an engineering pathology. 100% is unachievable, unmeasurable, and destroys the error budget mechanism entirely. The cost of pursuing it grows unboundedly while the user benefit asymptotes near zero.

runs.text: The SRE Book devotes significant attention to what it calls "the 100% availability trap" and the related "over-reliability" problem. The core argument:

items.text: Every system — hardware, software, network — has non-zero failure rates. The last few milliseconds of downtime that stand between 99.999% and 100% would require eliminating cosmic ray bit flips, hardware failures, and network partitions simultaneously. It is not a solvable engineering problem.

The SRE Book notes that users access services through multiple failure-prone layers: their device, their ISP, DNS, the CDN, TLS negotiation. The user-visible reliability of a service cannot exceed the reliability of the weakest link in their path to it — which is not your service. A 99.99% SLO is typically indistinguishable from 100% in user experience.
The error budget is zero, which breaks the model.

A 100% SLO means no error budget. Without an error budget, there is no room to deploy, no room to experiment, and no mechanism for the SRE / product team relationship to function. The entire SLO framework requires a non-zero budget.

Going from 99% to 99.9% may require $50K/year in infrastructure. Going from 99.9% to 99.99% may require $500K. Going from 99.99% to 99.999% may require $5M. Beyond some point, the engineering investment exceeds the business value of the incremental reliability.

runs.text: The right question is not "how reliable can we possibly make this?" but "how reliable does this need to be, given what users actually experience and what competitors provide?" The SRE Book calls this the
reliability target
— the minimum level of reliability that makes users happy, with any additional investment redirected to features.

Teams that target 100% SLOs typically end up with two problems simultaneously: they over-invest in reliability for non-critical services, and they under-invest in observability (because "we never go down"). The first wastes money; the second ensures that when they do go down, they cannot detect or recover from it.

Chasing 100% reliability costs exponentially more for each fraction of a percent gained, but users stop noticing improvements well before you reach 100%. Beyond a certain point, every dollar spent on reliability would be better spent on features that users can actually see. The error budget mechanism only works if the error budget is non-zero.

cards.title: User Journey SLOs — Beyond Single-Service Availability
cards.teaser: A single-service SLO answers whether one component is healthy. A user journey SLO answers whether the user can actually accomplish what they came to do — a checkout, a login, a report generation — end to end across multiple services.

runs.text: Most SLOs are defined per service: the API is 99.9% available, the database is 99.95% available, the CDN is 99.99% available. But users do not interact with services — they attempt
journeys

. A checkout journey touches the product catalog service, the inventory service, the payment service, the order service, and the notification service. If any one of them fails, the user cannot complete the checkout — even if every individual service SLO is green.
A
user journey SLO

measures the success rate of the end-to-end user action directly. The SLI is: "what fraction of checkout attempts resulted in a successful order within 30 seconds?" The SLO is: "99.5% of checkout attempts succeed."
The math of journey reliability is unforgiving:

A microservices architecture where every service has a three-nines SLO may produce a user-visible journey reliability of two nines or worse. This is why the SRE Workbook advocates measuring SLOs at the boundary closest to the user — the API gateway, the BFF (backend for frontend), or through synthetic monitoring that exercises the full journey.
Implementing user journey SLOs:

items.text: — scheduled real transactions (login, search, add to cart, checkout) that run continuously and emit success/failure metrics. These are the most accurate user journey SLIs because they exercise real code paths.
— instrumenting the client to emit journey completion events. High fidelity, but requires client-side instrumentation.
— correlating traces across services by journey type and computing end-to-end success rates from trace spans.

runs.text: The SRE Workbook recommends identifying your top 3-5 critical user journeys (the ones users care most about and that generate the most business value) and defining SLOs for each. Having per-journey SLOs alongside per-service SLOs allows you to triage incidents by user impact rather than by which microservice is alerting.

If 5 services each have 99.9% uptime, a user journey through all 5 is only available 99.5% of the time. Each hop multiplies the failure risk. A user journey SLO measures the whole path — whether the user actually succeeded — not just whether each piece of the plumbing was individually healthy.
